questions.q: Which arrow in Oja Market should be an event rather than a synchronous RPC call?
questions.explain: Nobody waits for a receipt, and a mail outage must not stop sales. The other three produce answers the customer or the next step needs right now.
options: gateway → auth: verifying the customer's token
orders → users: fetching the e-mail address for the order
orders → notifications: sending the receipt
gateway → orders: placing the order

questions.q: The notifications team needs the customer's e-mail address. What should they do?
questions.explain: A service's database is private to it. Reading it from outside couples two teams to one schema, so neither can change it without breaking the other.
options: Read it from the users service's database
Ask the users team for a read-only database login
Get it from an API or an event of the service that owns it; here, it travels inside the order.paid event
Store a hard-coded list of addresses

questions.q: The internal services have no public port. Why do they still check a service token on every RPC request?
questions.explain: Each service verifies who is calling. A token per service, or mutual TLS, even says which service it is, so payments can refuse anyone but orders.
options: Tokens make requests faster
"Not public" is not a control: a bug in the gateway or an attacker inside the network could call payments directly
The RPC package refuses to start without one
To count requests per service

questions.q: A frame's metadata carries traceparent. Why is it fine to take the trace from metadata, but not the user id?
questions.explain: Metadata is written by the caller, so it is untrusted. What decides access must come from something verified: the token check for the calling service, and a user id that a trusted service verified and passed in the validated input.
options: Metadata is encrypted for trace ids only
A forged trace id can only misplace a span; a forged user id would let the caller act as someone else
User ids are too long for metadata
The RPC server rejects user ids in metadata

questions.q: Why does serviceClient rethrow a timeout or a refused connection as RPCUnavailableError?
questions.explain: Only exposed errors keep their code across a service boundary. "A dependency did not answer" is useful to every caller up the chain, so it is turned into an error that says so.
options: To retry the call automatically
Otherwise the calling service would pass it upstream as an ordinary exception, the RPC server would hide it as RPC_INTERNAL_ERROR, and the customer would get a 500 instead of a 503
Because RPCTimeoutError cannot be caught
To hide the name of the failing service from logs

questions.q: Orders gives payments 1 second and users 2 seconds. What should the gateway's timeout for orders.place be?
questions.explain: If the gateway gives up first, the customer sees an error and retries while the first attempt may still succeed. Timeouts shrink as you go down the chain; passing a deadline down makes that automatic.
options: 1 second, the shortest one
The same as each of them, 2 seconds
More than orders' own calls added up, or the gateway gives up while orders is still working
No timeout at the gateway, because orders has timeouts

questions.q: Payments is down when Ada presses "Pay". What does Oja Market answer, and why?
questions.explain: 202 means accepted for processing. 201 would pretend it is paid; 402 would say the card was declined, which is not true; 500 would lose a sale that can still succeed.
options: 201, because the order will be charged later anyway
202 with status: "pending_payment": the order is accepted and honestly not paid yet
500, because a dependency failed
402, because the payment did not go through

questions.q: Payments charged the card, then its answer was lost in a timeout. Orders retries later. What stops a second charge?
questions.explain: The idempotency key travels with the operation to the system with the side effect. The queue's key only prevents two jobs from waiting at the same time; it knows nothing about what payments already did.
options: The retry queue's deduplicationKey
The charge carries the reference order-<id>; payments finds it in its records and returns the saved result
The timeout, which cancels the first charge
Nothing; the customer is refunded

questions.q: Where does the idempotency key for POST /orders come from?
questions.explain: A key made per request would differ for the second press and protect nothing. Only the client knows that two requests are the same cart. The key is scoped to the user, so one customer cannot collide with another.
options: The gateway generates a random one per request
The client sends it (Idempotency-Key), one per cart, so two presses of "Pay" carry the same key
Orders derives it from the current time
It is the user id

questions.q: Why does orders write order.paid to an outbox table instead of publishing it right after marking the order paid?
questions.explain: The relay publishes committed rows until it succeeds. The cost is that a row can be published twice, so consumers must be idempotent.
options: The broker is slower than PostgreSQL
The process can die between the update and the publish, and then a paid order never gets its event; with the outbox, both are in one transaction
Events must be sorted by id
So that notifications can read the orders database

questions.q: What does the serialization envelope add to the order.paid body?
questions.explain: With plain JSON, paidAt would arrive as a string without anyone noticing. The envelope's version also lets a consumer refuse a format it does not understand instead of misreading it.
options: Encryption of the payload
A format and version header, and type tags so that paidAt comes back as a Date
A signature that proves which service sent it
Compression

questions.q: Orders will start publishing order.paid version 2. In which order should the teams release?
questions.explain: If the producer goes first, every version 2 event lands in the consumers' rejected pile until they catch up. Consumers first, producers second, and never change the meaning of an existing field.
options: Orders first, then notifications
Notifications (every consumer) first, so it can read version 2 before anyone sends it
Both at exactly the same moment
It does not matter

questions.q: Notifications receives an event body that is not valid JSON. What should it do?
questions.explain: A broken body will be broken on every delivery. Retrying it forever blocks the events behind it; a person must look at it instead.
options: Throw, so the broker redelivers it until it works
Set it aside with the reason (a rejected list or a dead-letter queue) and move on to the next event
Send an empty receipt
Stop consuming until someone restarts the service

questions.q: The outbox relay published order 7's order.paid twice. Why does Ada still get one receipt?
questions.explain: Two layers: the queue refuses a second job for receipt-7 while the first exists, and the mail provider covers a duplicate that arrives after the first receipt went out.
options: The broker drops duplicates
The event bus only calls each handler once per type
The receipt job has a deduplication key while it waits, and the mail adapter ignores a key it already sent
Notifications keeps the last event only

questions.q: Notifications has no RPC procedures at all. What is the benefit?
questions.explain: A service that only reacts to events cannot be in anyone's critical path. The e-mail outage test proved it: orders were still answered with 201.
options: It uses less memory
No service depends on it synchronously, so its outages can only delay receipts, never block an order
It cannot be attacked
It does not need a queue

questions.q: The payment retry job stores traceparent in its data. What would be lost without it?
questions.explain: AsyncLocalStorage does not survive a queue. Every asynchronous hop (queue job, outbox row, broker message) must carry the trace context explicitly.
options: The retry would not run
The retry would start a new trace, so the successful charge, the event and the receipt would not appear under the trace id the customer was given
The charge would happen twice
The order would stay pending_payment

questions.q: Why does the gateway put the trace id in an x-trace-id response header?
questions.explain: A trace id is not a secret and reveals nothing about the data. It is the handle that turns "my order failed at 14:03" into one trace.
options: Browsers need it to cache responses
Support can ask the customer for it and find the whole request across every service with one search
It proves the response is authentic
It makes the next request faster

questions.q: While payments is down, each order still waits a full second for the payments timeout before it becomes pending_payment. What fixes that?
questions.explain: The breaker turns a slow failure into a fast one while the dependency is known to be down, and lets one trial call through to notice when it is back.
options: A longer timeout
A circuit breaker that, after a few failures, skips the call and goes straight to the retry queue until a trial call succeeds
Retrying inside the request
Removing the timeout

questions.q: Why does orders compute the total from its own price list instead of taking prices from the cart the client sent?
questions.explain: The body says what the customer wants: which products and how many. What things cost is the shop's data.
options: Prices from clients are always in the wrong currency
The client controls the request body, so a price from it would let anyone set their own price
Because JSON cannot hold integers
To save one database query

questions.q: Orders calls users for every order. What is the trade-off of keeping a copy of each customer's e-mail inside orders instead?
questions.explain: Removing a synchronous dependency buys availability with eventual consistency. The owner of the address is still users; orders only holds a copy it updates from user.updated.
options: No trade-off: copies are always better
Orders keeps selling when users is down, but its copy can be slightly out of date and must be kept current from events
It makes orders the owner of the e-mail address
It removes the need for a users service

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Inside the envelope the date is a tagged object, { "$type": "Date", "$value": … }. Parsing the data with plain JSON.parse gives that object; only the matching serializer turns it back into a Date. Producer and consumer must agree on the format, which is what the envelope records.
options: object true
string true
object false
string false

questions.q: A consumer receives an envelope from a newer producer. What does this print?
questions.explain: The envelope's own format version is checked before the data is read, so an old consumer fails loudly instead of misreading a newer layout.
options: refused: Unsupported envelope schema version 2: this build understands up to 1
accepted
refused: Unexpected end of JSON input
refused: Envelope format mismatch: expected "json", got "json"

questions.q: The consumer checks the payload's v field. What does this print?
questions.explain: A missing version is not "version 1": it is an event of unknown shape. Refusing it is safer than guessing.
options:
receipt for order 7
rejected: unsupported order.paid version 2
rejected: unsupported order.paid version undefined

receipt for order 7
receipt for order 8
receipt for order 9

receipt for order 7
receipt for order 8
rejected: unsupported order.paid version undefined

receipt for order 7
rejected: unsupported order.paid version 2
receipt for order 9

questions.q: Two copies of the same event arrive while the first receipt job is still waiting. What does this print?
questions.explain: The deduplication key refuses a second job while the first exists. JobDuplicateError is imported from @zudojs/errors, where the queue's errors are defined.
options:
delivery 1: queued
delivery 2: already queued
waiting: 1

delivery 1: queued
delivery 2: queued
waiting: 2

delivery 1: queued
delivery 2: already queued
waiting: 2

delivery 1: already queued
delivery 2: already queued
waiting: 0

questions.q: A payments service keeps charges by reference. What does this print?
questions.explain: The retry of order-41 is answered from the records; only a new reference reaches the card processor. In the lesson the records live in a database, so they also survive a restart.
options: ch_1 true 2
ch_2 false 3
ch_1 false 2
ch_1 true 3

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The header carries the trace id and the caller's span id, so the server's span joins the same trace as a child of the call. A malformed header gives undefined, and a span started with it begins a fresh trace.
options:
true true
undefined

true false
undefined

false false
null

true true
{}

questions.q: The gateway picks the status from the order's state. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each state gets the status that tells the truth: created and paid, accepted but not paid yet, and payment required because the card was declined.
questions.code:
const statusFor = (order) => (order.status === "paid" ? 201 : order.status === "pending_payment" ? 202 : 402);

console.log(["paid", "pending_payment", "declined"].map((status) => statusFor({ status })));

questions.q: Two consumers listen to order.paid and one of them fails. What does this print?
questions.explain: One failing consumer does not stop the others, and the result names it. In the lesson, notifications does not throw on a mail failure at all: it queues the receipt and lets the queue retry.
options:
loyalty: points added
1 1 [ 'notifications' ]
1 1 [ 'notifications' ]

loyalty: points added
2 0 []
Error: SMTP connection refused

questions.q: Orders retries payments with this backoff. What does this print?
questions.explain: The wait doubles from 200 ms and is capped at 5 seconds. Seven retries cover about 16 seconds of outage; a longer outage needs a longer schedule, or the order stays pending for a person to look at.

questions.q: A consumer decodes three bodies. What does this print?
questions.explain: Both bad events are set aside with a reason, in the order they arrived, and the consumer keeps going. Checking SyntaxError avoids printing the engine's parser message, which differs between runtimes.
options:
[ 'ok 7', 'set aside', 'set aside' ]
[ 'version 2', 'not JSON' ]

[ 'ok 7', 'ok 8', 'set aside' ]
[ 'not JSON' ]

[ 'ok 7', 'set aside', 'set aside' ]
[ 'not JSON', 'version 2' ]

[ 'ok 7' ]
[ 'version 2', 'not JSON' ]

questions.q: Write checkServiceToken(header, expected) that returns true only when header is exactly "Bearer " + expected, comparing in constant time: compare every character (even after a mismatch) and the lengths. Print the result for the right token, a wrong one, a missing header and a prefix of the right one.
questions.explain: A comparison that stops at the first different character answers faster for a worse guess, and an attacker can measure that. The lesson uses timingSafeEqualString from @zudojs/crypto, which does this for you.

questions.q: Write httpStatusFor(rpcCode) for the gateway: RPC_UNAUTHENTICATED → 401, RPC_NOT_FOUND → 404, RPC_VALIDATION_ERROR → 400, RPC_UNAVAILABLE, RPC_TIMEOUT and RPC_TRANSPORT_ERROR → 503, anything else → 500. Print the statuses for the sample codes, separated by spaces.
questions.explain: The gateway translates between two vocabularies. "A service did not answer" is a 503 the client may retry; an internal error is a 500 without details.

questions.q: Write createLoyalty() returning { onOrderPaid(event), points(email) }. It awards one point per ₦1,000 (100,000 kobo, rounded down) and ignores an orderId it has already handled. Deliver order 7 (2,850,000 kobo) twice and order 8 (350,000 kobo) once for the same e-mail, and print the points.
questions.explain: 28 + 3 points, with the duplicate delivery ignored. At-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer is the normal, reliable combination.

questions.q: Write relay(outbox, publish): for every row with publishedAt === null, in id order, call publish(row) and then set publishedAt. Return how many rows it published. Run it twice and print both counts and the published topics.
questions.explain: Publishing before marking means a crash in between publishes the row again next time: at least once, never zero times. The reverse order could lose the event.

questions.q: Write placeOrder(order, chargeFn, retryQueue). It calls chargeFn(order): on "succeeded" the order becomes paid, on "declined" it becomes declined. If chargeFn throws an error whose code is "RPC_UNAVAILABLE", the order becomes pending_payment and its id is pushed to retryQueue; any other error is rethrown. Print the three cases.
questions.explain: Only "did not answer" is turned into a later retry; a real error, such as a bug, still fails loudly. The retry is safe because the charge carries the order's reference.

questions.q: Write servicesInTrace(spans, traceId) that returns the sorted, unique service names of the spans that belong to traceId. Print it for the sample spans.
questions.explain: This is the heart of the lesson's trace test: if a hop forgets to pass the traceparent, its service drops out of this list and the test names it.

questions.q: A type argument on an RPC call is not checked at runtime. Use @zudojs/schema to validate the answer from users.get: an object with a string userId and a string email. Print whether each of the two sample answers is valid.
questions.explain: The second answer is what users might send after its team renamed a field. With the schema, orders fails clearly at the boundary instead of saving an order with an undefined e-mail address.

questions.q: The relay publishes a row, then crashes before it marks the row published. After a restart it runs again. What does this print?
questions.explain: The event was delivered twice, which is what "at least once" means. The consumer keyed its work by order id, so the customer still got one receipt.

questions.q: A cart arrives with prices in it. What does this print?
questions.explain: The trusting total lets the customer pay ₦3 for ₦28,500 of groceries. The body says what the customer wants; the price comes from the service that owns it.

questions.q: Orders keeps a local copy of e-mail addresses, updated from user.updated events. Events can arrive twice or out of order, so each carries a version that grows with every change. Write apply(copy, event) that stores { email, version } for event.userId only when the event's version is newer than the stored one. Apply the sample events in order and print the copy.
questions.explain: The late version 2 would otherwise overwrite the newer address. Comparing versions makes the copy both idempotent (the repeated version 3) and safe against reordering.
